Prefrontal default-mode network interactions with posterior hippocampus during exploration

Flexible prefrontal control over hippocampal episodic memory for goal-directed generalization

Fronto-Hippocampal Synchronization in Rapid Spatial Learning in Humans

The hippocampal formation supplies a fast, recombinable code for episodes and relations-a substrate for scene construction, counterfactuals, and prospective imagination-while the prefrontal cortex (PFC) provides goal-directed control over when and how those internal models are consulted. A robust macro-level regularity is that hippocampus couples with the default-mode network (DMN) during retrieval and simulation and decouples during externally focused encoding 4, 5, consistent with a control policy that engages internal models when they help and suppresses them when sensory-driven control is required. Reward prediction errors during a decision task predict later recognition memory (Figure) 26. Hippocampal activity during recognition reactivates anterior-cingulate error representations (Figure).

What is exchanged between hippocampus and PFC during "imagination" is not raw sensory replay but brief, structured trajectories over a learned state-relation graph. Hippocampal sharp-wave ripples and theta-nested sequences compress experience into forward and reverse rollouts; these events recruit distributed control networks and can bias upcoming choices 6. In humans, magnetoencephalography (MEG) reveals sub-second replay of candidate paths that ramps up before decisions when planning is beneficial; across rest and task, replay bursts co-activate hippocampus with DMN hubs 7, suggesting a system-level channel for internal evaluation 8.

When-and how strongly-PFC queries the hippocampal "world model" appears to follow an expected-value-of-computation (EVOC) principle. Normative accounts predict that agents prioritize the memories whose evaluation most improves reward rate; hippocampal replay in rodents and humans follows this prioritization, emphasizing reward-salient or task-relevant paths, and human replay strength scales with planning demand 9, 10. This yields a concrete control objective for PFC: regulate access to hippocampal simulation based on opportunity cost and expected utility 11.

Circuit anatomy makes this gating feasible. Ventral CA1/subiculum conveys contextual state directly to medial PFC (mPFC) and amygdala, supporting valuation and control over behaviorally significant contexts 12. In the top-down direction, the thalamic nucleus reuniens (RE) is a key relay from PFC to hippocampus and entorhinal cortex; perturbing RE alters PFC-hippocampal synchrony and memory performance, and, during memory-guided decisions, RE can drive transient beta-band coupling that appears to "bind" PFC and hippocampus into a single control loop 13, 14. Functionally, PFC->RE->HPC acts as a broadcast channel for turning simulation on/off and for routing which memories are sampled.

Beyond glutamatergic relays, there is a direct long-range GABAergic projection from PFC to hippocampus 15. Activating these PFC->HPC inhibitory axons increases feedforward inhibition and improves hippocampal signal-to-noise for location coding, providing a rapid, cell-type-specific lever for top-down suppression or sharpening of hippocampal activity during externally anchored tasks-essentially, a concrete circuit for "retrieval stopping" and noise gating 15.

Timing gives PFC additional control surfaces. During NREM sleep and quiet wake, sequential slow-oscillation->spindle->ripple cascades orchestrate hippocampal-cortical dialogue; spindles provide the temporal window in which ripples convey reactivated content to cortex, and replay-locked events can propagate cortex-wide 16. New intracranial work in humans shows that brief prefrontal "cortical ripples" can impose top-down modulation of hippocampal reactivation, suggesting a fast timing-based veto when reactivation would be maladaptive 17, 18. A practical design lesson is to decompose fast hippocampal rollouts from slower prefrontal timing controllers that gate when-and for how long-simulation runs.

PFC also suppresses hippocampal output when attention must remain sensorimotor-locked or when intrusive traces 19 threaten performance. Think/No-Think studies show that lateral PFC down-regulates hippocampus to stop retrieval, with concomitant amygdala down-regulation for aversive content 20; related rodent work indicates that RE-mediated synchrony helps suppress extinguished fear 21. Together with the long-range GABAergic pathway, these findings specify multiple levers-oscillatory timing, thalamic gating, and direct inhibition-by which PFC enforces task-appropriate access to internal simulations.

Functionally, PFC and hippocampus bring complementary inductive biases. The hippocampus is optimized for rapidly encoding and recombining specific episodes (it "knows" where you are in a rich state-space and can imagine novel arrangements on the fly). PFC, by contrast, is geared toward abstract, goal-oriented control and working memory. A recent theory formalizes PFC working memory as controllable, structured activity "slots" that interface naturally with hippocampal cognitive maps-an algorithmic duality between activity-based WM and synaptic episodic memory 22. In practice, PFC can retrieve an episode, hold and transform it within slot-like subspaces, bind it to current goals/values, and then decide whether more rollouts are worth the compute 23. This synergy lets an animal generalize from a single experience: PFC can "plug in" an episodic memory into its current goal context, recombine it with other memories, and thus plan new behavior without extensive new learning. Empirical studies highlight this benefit. For example, hippocampal replay-PFC coordination supports both recalling useful past routes and exploring new shortcuts in a maze 24, and models predict that this interplay can explain flexible transfer to novel tasks (compositional generalization) 25.

Overall, we can treat the PFC-hippocampal system as a controller-simulator pair. Represent the world as a hierarchical predictive graph (SR-like) in the simulator; let the controller learn an EVOC policy that gates rollouts via (i) a thalamic-like broadcast (RE) that sets when simulation is allowed, (ii) timing windows that schedule rollouts into oscillatory "slots," and (iii) a direct inhibitory path that suppresses or sharpens retrieval when external demands dominate.
